```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import statsmodels.api as sm
import ruptures as rpt

from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import breaks_cusumolsresid, breaks_hansen
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import recursive_olsresiduals

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="talk")
plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = (10, 5)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 30)
pd.set_option("display.width", 140)

COLORS = {
    "data": "#6B7280",
    "primary": "#0072B2",
    "break": "#CC3311",
    "regime": "#D55E00",
    "monitor": "#009E73",
}

# Public, built-in dataset from statsmodels.
nile = sm.datasets.nile.load_pandas().data.copy()
nile["year"] = nile["year"].astype(int)
nile["time"] = np.arange(len(nile))
signal = nile["volume"].to_numpy()

# Stable intercept-only reference model used for parameter-stability tests.
X_level = np.ones((len(nile), 1))
level_model = sm.OLS(nile["volume"], X_level).fit()

# Package-based offline change-point detection.
pelt_l2 = rpt.Pelt(model="l2", min_size=10, jump=1).fit(signal)
pelt_rbf = rpt.Pelt(model="rbf", min_size=10, jump=1).fit(signal)
binseg = rpt.Binseg(model="l2", min_size=10, jump=1).fit(signal)
dynp = rpt.Dynp(model="l2", min_size=10, jump=1).fit(signal)
window = rpt.Window(width=20, model="l2", min_size=10, jump=1).fit(signal)
bottomup = rpt.BottomUp(model="l2", min_size=10, jump=1).fit(signal)

# Breakpoint lists include the terminal sample index by ruptures convention.
pelt_pen_5 = pelt_l2.predict(pen=5_000)
pelt_pen_10 = pelt_l2.predict(pen=10_000)
pelt_pen_20 = pelt_l2.predict(pen=20_000)
pelt_rbf_breaks = pelt_rbf.predict(pen=4)
binseg_one = binseg.predict(n_bkps=1)
dynp_one = dynp.predict(n_bkps=1)
window_one = window.predict(n_bkps=1)
bottomup_one = bottomup.predict(n_bkps=1)

method_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "method": ["PELT L2", "PELT RBF", "Binary segmentation", "Dynamic programming", "Window", "Bottom-up"],
    "break_index": [pelt_pen_10[-2], pelt_rbf_breaks[-2], binseg_one[-2], dynp_one[-2], window_one[-2], bottomup_one[-2]],
})
method_results["break_year"] = method_results["break_index"].map(
    lambda i: int(nile.iloc[i]["year"])
)
dynp_breaks = (
    rpt.Dynp(
        model="l2",
        min_size=10,
        jump=1,
    )
    .fit(signal)
    .predict(n_bkps=1)
)
```

# Introduction

## Why change points matter

Structural changes alter the distribution or model relationship of a time series.

They can make older data less representative for:

- forecasting;
- monitoring;
- policy evaluation;
- risk estimation;
- anomaly detection;
- model calibration.

::: {.notes}
The supplied Towards Data Science article defines a change point as the timestep marking the onset of a distributional change and notes that historical data may become less representative after a change.

[Sources]
- https://towardsdatascience.com/understanding-time-series-structural-changes-f6a4c44cb13c/
:::

## Learning objectives

Students will be able to:

- distinguish change points from outliers;
- identify changes in mean, variance, and model parameters;
- use built-in data from `statsmodels`;
- apply package implementations from `ruptures`;
- perform CUSUM and Hansen stability tests with `statsmodels`;
- compare PELT, binary segmentation, dynamic programming, window, and bottom-up methods;
- communicate uncertainty and tuning sensitivity visually.

::: {.notes}
This version intentionally uses established Python packages instead of implementing change-point algorithms manually.
:::

## Structural change versus outlier

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Outlier

An isolated observation that is unusual relative to the prevailing structure.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Structural change

A persistent change in the underlying distribution or model relationship.
:::
:::

> A large observation can be an outlier without creating a new regime.

::: {.notes}
The supplied article explicitly distinguishes outliers from change points: an outlier differs from normal behavior, while a change point alters the structure to a different distribution.

[Sources]
- https://towardsdatascience.com/understanding-time-series-structural-changes-f6a4c44cb13c/
:::

## Types of structural change

- permanent change in mean;
- transitory change in mean;
- permanent change in variance;
- transitory change in variance;
- volatility clustering;
- changing regression coefficients;
- changing autoregressive dynamics.

::: {.notes}
The supplied article discusses permanent and transitory mean changes, variance changes, and volatility clustering. Regression-parameter instability is the focus of the strucchange framework.

[Sources]
- https://towardsdatascience.com/understanding-time-series-structural-changes-f6a4c44cb13c/
- https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/strucchange/strucchange.pdf
:::

## Two complementary perspectives

| Perspective | Question | Python package |
|---|---|---|
| Parameter stability | Did a specified model remain stable? | `statsmodels` |
| Offline segmentation | Where does the signal divide into different regimes? | `ruptures` |

::: {.notes}
The strucchange framework considers stability of model parameters. Ruptures is designed for offline change-point detection and segmentation of non-stationary signals.

[Sources]
- https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/strucchange/strucchange.pdf
- https://centre-borelli.github.io/ruptures-docs/
:::

# Known and Reproducible Data

## Nile River dataset

The dataset records annual Nile River discharge at Aswan:

- years: 1871–1970;
- observations: 100;
- measurement units: billions of cubic metres;
- a widely documented apparent change near 1898.

```{python}
nile.head()
```

::: {.notes}
Statsmodels documents the Nile dataset as annual river volume at Aswan from 1871 to 1970, with 100 observations and an apparent change point near 1898.

[Sources]
- https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/dev/dataset_notes.html
:::

## Visual inspection

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(nile["year"], nile["volume"], marker="o", markersize=3, color=COLORS["primary"])
ax.set(title="Annual Nile River volume at Aswan", xlabel="Year", ylabel=r"Volume ($10^9$ m³)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The raw chart suggests a change in the average level, but visual inspection alone does not determine the method, number of breaks, or uncertainty.
:::

## Before-and-after summaries are descriptive

```{python}
summary_1898 = (
    nile.assign(period=np.where(nile["year"] < 1898, "Before 1898", "1898 onward"))
    .groupby("period")["volume"]
    .agg(["count", "mean", "std", "median"])
)
summary_1898
```

::: {.notes}
The year 1898 is used as a documented reference point from the statsmodels dataset description. This summary is descriptive, not a formal test.

[Sources]
- https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/dev/dataset_notes.html
:::

## Distribution view by period

```{python}
plot_data = nile.assign(
    period=np.where(nile["year"] < 1898, "Before 1898", "1898 onward")
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.boxplot(data=plot_data, x="period", y="volume", hue="period", legend=False, ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Distribution before and after the documented reference year", xlabel="", ylabel=r"Volume ($10^9$ m³)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Grouping by a known historical reference is useful for description, but package-based change-point methods should estimate break locations without assuming the answer.
:::


## Stable mean as an intercept-only model

$$
y_t=\beta_0+u_t.
$$

```{python}
level_model.summary().tables[1]
```

This model asks whether one mean level describes the entire sample.

::: {.notes}
Using an intercept-only model translates level stability into parameter stability. More complex regressions can be assessed using the same testing logic.
:::

## OLS-CUSUM with `statsmodels`

```{python}
cusum_stat, cusum_pvalue, cusum_critical = breaks_cusumolsresid(
    level_model.resid,
    ddof=len(level_model.params),
)

pd.Series({
    "CUSUM statistic": cusum_stat,
    "p-value": cusum_pvalue,
    "critical values": cusum_critical,
})
```

::: {.notes}
The calculation uses the statsmodels diagnostic function rather than a handwritten CUSUM test.
:::

## Hansen stability test

```{python}
hansen_stat, hansen_critical = breaks_hansen(level_model)

pd.Series({
    "Hansen statistic": hansen_stat,
    "critical values": hansen_critical,
})
```

::: {.notes}
This slide uses the statsmodels Hansen stability test on the fitted OLS model. Interpretation should follow the test output and its documented critical values.
:::

## Recursive OLS diagnostics

```{python}
recursive_output = recursive_olsresiduals(
    level_model,
    skip=3,
    alpha=0.95,
)

recursive_resid = recursive_output[0]
recursive_cusum = recursive_output[5]
recursive_ci = recursive_output[6]
```

The package returns recursive residuals, a cumulative process, and confidence limits.

::: {.notes}
The analysis uses the statsmodels recursive OLS diagnostic routine. No recursive-residual formula is implemented manually in the presentation.
:::

## Recursive CUSUM visualization

```{python}
recursive_years = nile["year"].iloc[-len(recursive_cusum):].to_numpy()
boundary_years = recursive_years[1:]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(recursive_years, recursive_cusum, color=COLORS["primary"], label="Recursive CUSUM")
ax.plot(boundary_years, recursive_ci[0], color=COLORS["break"], linestyle="--", label="95% limits")
ax.plot(boundary_years, recursive_ci[1], color=COLORS["break"], linestyle="--")
ax.set(title="Recursive OLS stability process", xlabel="Year", ylabel="CUSUM")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The process and confidence limits are returned by statsmodels. A crossing indicates that the recursive process is inconsistent with stability at the selected confidence level.
:::

# Data Visualization Guidance

## Show the raw signal and regimes together

A useful chart includes:

- the original signal;
- estimated change dates;
- regime shading or fitted segment means;
- the method and cost model;
- tuning parameters;
- units and observation frequency.

::: {.notes}
Ruptures emphasizes display of signals and estimated change points. The source article also presents the detected regimes visually.

[Sources]
- https://centre-borelli.github.io/ruptures-docs/
- https://towardsdatascience.com/understanding-time-series-structural-changes-f6a4c44cb13c/
:::

## Plot segment means

```{python}
chosen_breaks = dynp_breaks
segment_starts = [0] + chosen_breaks[:-1]
segment_ends = chosen_breaks

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(nile["year"], nile["volume"], color="0.75", label="Observed")
for number, (start, end) in enumerate(zip(segment_starts, segment_ends), start=1):
    subset = nile.iloc[start:end]
    ax.hlines(subset["volume"].mean(), subset["year"].iloc[0], subset["year"].iloc[-1],
              color=sns.color_palette("Set1")[number - 1], linewidth=3,
              label=f"Regime {number} mean")
for index in chosen_breaks[:-1]:
    ax.axvline(nile.iloc[index]["year"], color=COLORS["break"], linestyle="--")
ax.set(title="Observed series and estimated regime means", xlabel="Year", ylabel=r"Volume ($10^9$ m³)")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
This chart uses package-estimated breakpoints and pandas summaries. It does not reimplement the change-point search.
:::

## Always label the detection target

State whether the analysis targets:

- mean shifts;
- median shifts;
- variance changes;
- distributional changes;
- autoregressive parameter changes;
- regression coefficient changes.

A line labeled only “structural break” is underspecified.

::: {.notes}
The supplied article distinguishes level and variance changes, while ruptures exposes different cost models for different segmentation objectives.

[Sources]
- https://towardsdatascience.com/understanding-time-series-structural-changes-f6a4c44cb13c/
- https://centre-borelli.github.io/ruptures-docs/
:::

# Interpretation and Response

## What can be done after a detected change?

Possible responses include:

- retrain models on recent regimes;
- add intervention or regime indicators;
- use differencing for level instability;
- transform variance;
- fit regime-switching models;
- monitor for future changes;
- investigate operational or measurement events.

::: {.notes}
The supplied article mentions differencing, dummy variables, preprocessing for variance changes, and regime-switching models as possible responses. The appropriate response depends on the change type and business context.

[Sources]
- https://towardsdatascience.com/understanding-time-series-structural-changes-f6a4c44cb13c/
:::

## Intervention indicator after a dated change

```{python}
reference_year = int(method_results["break_year"].mode().iloc[0])
nile["post_change"] = (nile["year"] >= reference_year).astype(int)
intervention_model = sm.OLS(
    nile["volume"],
    sm.add_constant(nile[["post_change"]]),
).fit()
intervention_model.summary().tables[1]
```

::: {.notes}
This uses statsmodels to estimate a simple level-shift intervention after a package-derived reference date. It describes the shift but does not establish causality.
:::

## Differencing changes the question

```{python}
nile["difference"] = nile["volume"].diff()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(11, 6))
axes[0].plot(nile["year"], nile["volume"], color=COLORS["primary"])
axes[0].set_ylabel("Level")
axes[1].plot(nile["year"], nile["difference"], color=COLORS["monitor"])
axes[1].axhline(0, color="0.4", linewidth=1)
axes[1].set(xlabel="Year", ylabel="First difference")
fig.suptitle("Levels and first differences")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The supplied article notes that differencing can stabilize mean-level changes. Differencing also changes the analytical target from levels to increments.

[Sources]
- https://towardsdatascience.com/understanding-time-series-structural-changes-f6a4c44cb13c/
:::

# Common Errors

## Change-point failure modes

- treating a single outlier as a new regime;
- applying a mean-shift cost to a variance-change question;
- choosing a penalty only because the result looks attractive;
- hiding disagreement between algorithms;
- forgetting that `ruptures` returns the terminal endpoint;
- reporting an estimated date as an exact historical fact;
- using the full sample to tune an online detector;
- claiming causal effects from segmentation alone;
- ignoring seasonality or autocorrelation;
- presenting one package default as a universal answer.

::: {.notes}
These cautions combine the distinctions in the source article with the tuning and segmentation structure documented by ruptures.
:::

# Practice

## Classroom exercise

Using the built-in Nile dataset:

1. plot the original series;
2. apply OLS-CUSUM and Hansen stability tests;
4. compare three penalty levels;
7. visualize regime means;
8. estimate a post-change indicator model;
9. explain method disagreement;
10. state what cannot be concluded causally.

::: {.notes}
The exercise is fully replicable because the series ships through statsmodels and the calculations use documented package methods.
:::

# Key Takeaways

## Main conclusions

1. Structural changes alter the distribution or model relationship.
2. Outliers and change points are different concepts.
3. `statsmodels` provides stability tests and reproducible datasets.
4. `ruptures` provides multiple offline segmentation algorithms.
5. The cost model defines what type of change is being detected.
6. PELT requires an explicit penalty choice.
7. Other algorithms can condition on a specified number of changes.
8. Method disagreement is useful diagnostic evidence.
9. Sensitivity analysis belongs in the visualization.
10. Detection does not establish causality.

::: {.notes}
The package ecosystem provides tools for different but complementary structural-change questions.

[Sources]
- https://towardsdatascience.com/understanding-time-series-structural-changes-f6a4c44cb13c/

:::
